Thus the awe and consideration that we grant to the outcast and to those who take refuge with us gods is something honored by Zeus himself (cf. his behavior toward Ixion at 717 f., and ⟦9⟧ the chorus against Apollo at 151; below on 233 f.), and with ⟦10⟧ Hermes now sets out as escort of Orestes. Apollo also departs, unclear to where; in the following scene he is certainly not present. Now there appears before the sleeping Erinyes, raised up by the ⟦11⟧ (Pollux 4, 132), the ghost of Clytemnestra, according to 116 ⟦12⟧, 155 ⟦13⟧ the sensory embodiment of a dream that the sleepers are having; between dream and actual ghostly apparition it is mediated by the fact that in sleep the heart is clairvoyant, 104 f. Cf. in Homer the ⟦14⟧, who takes the form of Nestor, B 20 ff., and the dream vision of Penelope ⟦15⟧ 795 ff., an ⟦16⟧ in the form of her sister. Yet from Homer the appearance of the soul of Patroclus Ψ 65 ff. compares even more closely, where Achilles sleeps, while there is no talk of a dream, but only of the actual soul; what it says is very similar to the words of Clytemnestra here: ⟦17⟧, ⟦18⟧.
